{{Short description|Formal language theorem}}
In [[formal language theory]], the '''Büchi–Elgot–Trakhtenbrot theorem''' states that a language is [[regular language|regular]] if and only if it can be defined by a formula in [[monadic second-order logic]] (MSO). The theorem is due to [[Julius Richard Büchi]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Büchi |first1=Julius Richard |title=Weak second order arithmetic and finite automata |journal=Zeitschrift für Mathematische Logik und Grundlagen der Mathematik |date=1960 |volume=6 |issue=1–6 |pages=66–92|doi=10.1002/malq.19600060105 }}</ref> [[Calvin Elgot]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Elgot |first1=Calvin C. |title=Decision problems of finite automata design and related arithmetics |journal=[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=1961 |volume=98 |pages=21–52|doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1961-0139530-9 |s2cid=119721061 |doi-access=free |hdl=2027.42/4758 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> and [[Boris Trakhtenbrot]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Trakhtenbrot |first1=Boris A. |title=Конечные автоматы и логика одноместных предикатов |language=Russian |trans-title=Finite automata and the logic of one-place predicates |journal=[[Siberian Mathematical Journal]] |date=1962 |volume=3 |pages=103–131}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Trakhtenbrot |first1=Boris A. |title=Finite automata and the logic of one-place predicates |journal=American Mathematical Society Translations |series=American Mathematical Society Translations: Series 2 |date=1966 |volume=59 |pages=23–55|doi=10.1090/trans2/059/02 |isbn=9780821817599 }}</ref>

Since a language is regular if and only if it can be defined as the accepted language of a [[Finite-state machine|finite-state automaton]], a more precise statement of the theorem is that for every MSO formula defining a formal language, we can find a finite-state automaton defining the same language, and for every finite-state automaton, we can find an MSO formula defining the same language.

== Examples ==
Regular languages are usually described by [[regular expression]]s. For instance, <math>(ab)^*</math> represents the regular language of words where the pattern <math>ab</math> is repeated:

:<math>\epsilon, ab, abab, ababab, abababab, \ldots </math>

The same language is represented by the following monadic second-order logic formula (in this case a [[first-order logic]] formula). The variables represent word indices (positions), and the predicate <math>S(x, y)</math> denotes the successor relation <math>y = x + 1</math>.

:<math>\begin{array}{l}
(\exists x \; \forall y \; \lnot S(y, x) \land a(x)) \\
\land (\exists x \; \forall y \; \lnot S(x, y) \land b(x)) \\
\land (\forall x \forall y \; (S(x,y) \land a(x)) \rightarrow b(y)) \\
\land (\forall x \forall y \; (S(x,y) \land b(x)) \rightarrow a(y)) \\
\end{array}</math>

In words:
* There is a position <math>x</math> which is the beginning of the word and has letter <math>a</math>.
* There is a position <math>x</math> which is the end of the word and has letter <math>b</math>.
* Any position following a letter <math>a</math> must have letter <math>b</math>.
* Any position following a letter <math>b</math> must have letter <math>a</math>.

A second example is the regular expression <math>(aa)^*</math>. This language cannot be expressed in first-order logic and needs the second-order quantification of MSO. We introduce an <math>\text{EVEN}</math> predicate that is exactly true on positions that are even. The following MSO formula says that all letters are <math>a</math>, that <math>\text{EVEN}</math> is true at every even index, and that <math>\text{EVEN}</math> is true at the ending position.

:<math>\begin{array}{l}
(\forall x \; a(x)) \land \exists \text{EVEN} \\
 (\exists x \; \forall y \; \lnot S(y, x) \land \lnot \text{EVEN}(x)) \\
\land (\exists x \; \forall y \; \lnot S(x, y) \land \text{EVEN}(x)) \\
\land (\forall x \forall y \; (S(x,y) \land \text{EVEN}(x)) \rightarrow \lnot\text{EVEN}(y)) \\
\land (\forall x \forall y \; (S(x,y) \land \lnot\text{EVEN}(x)) \rightarrow \text{EVEN}(y)) \\
\end{array}</math>

== Setup ==
Let <math>\Sigma</math> be a finite nonempty set, called the [[Alphabet (formal languages)|alphabet]]. A formal language is a subset of <math>\Sigma^*</math>, the set of finite-length strings formed by elements of <math>\Sigma</math>. A language is regular if and only if it is accepted by a finite-state automaton.

In order to define languages using logical formulas, we need the following logical formalism. Other than the first-order logic symbols, it also has the following predicates:

* The equality relation <math>=</math>.
* One monadic relation <math>Q_a</math> per letter <math>a \in \Sigma</math>, where <math>Q_a(x)</math> means "location <math>x</math> contains letter <math>a</math>". 
* The successor relation <math>S(x, y)</math>, meaning "location <math>x</math> is immediately followed by location <math>y</math>".
** Since in MSO logic we can quantify over all monadic predicates, the successor relation can be used to define an ordering relation <math>x < y</math> as the [[transitive closure]] of <math>S(x, y)</math>:<math display="block">\neg x = y \wedge \forall X (X(x) \wedge \forall z, z' (X(z) \wedge S(z, z') \to X(z') ) \to X(y))</math>This construction is similar to the induction principle in Peano arithmetic.

With this formalism, one can characterize a language by a single MSO formula <math>\sigma</math>. Specifically, <math>\sigma</math> defines the set <math>L_\sigma := \{w \in \Sigma^* : M_w \models \sigma\}</math>. In this definition, to each word <math>w \in \Sigma^*</math>, we define a [[Finite model theory|finite model]] <math>M_w</math> with the following conditions:

* The universe of <math>M_w</math> is <math>\{1, 2, \dots, |w|\}</math>.
* For each <math>n \in \{1, 2, \dots, |w|\}</math>, we have <math>M_w \models Q_a(n)</math> if and only if <math>w_n = a </math>.
* For each <math>n,m \in \{1, 2, \dots, |w|\}</math>, we have <math>M_w \models S(n,m)</math> if and only if <math>m = n+1</math>.

Any such language <math>L_\sigma</math> is said to be MSO-expressible.

== Theorem statement ==
A language <math>L \subseteq \Sigma^*</math> is regular iff it is MSO-expressible.

== Proof overview ==

=== Regular implies MSO-expressible ===
Given a regular language <math>L</math>, it is specified by a finite-state automaton with <math>k</math> states. Then, one constructs a MSO formula of the form <math>\exists X_1, \dots, X_k, \phi(X_1, \dots, X_k)</math>. Here, each <math>X_i</math> is supposed to be interpreted as the set of locations at which the automaton is at state <math>i</math>. The formula <math>\phi(X_1, \dots, X_k)</math> then expresses the following:

* Any location belongs to exactly one of <math>X_1, \dots, X_k</math>, and
* the state transition at each location follows the automaton's edge rules, and
* the last location is in one of the accepting states.

More concretely, we can construct the formula as a conjunction of the following:

* <math>\forall x, \bigvee_{i: 1 \leq i \leq n}\left(X_i(x)\wedge\bigwedge_{j : j \neq i, 1 \leq j \leq n} \neg X_j(x)\right) </math>.
* <math>\forall x, y, S(x, y) \to \bigvee_{i: 1 \leq i \leq n, a \in \Sigma} X_i(x) \wedge Q_a(x) \wedge X_{A(i, a)}(y)   </math>, where we use <math>A(i, a)   </math> to mean: the state you arrive at, if you start at state <math>i   </math> on the automaton and follow the edge for letter <math>a   </math>.
** In this part, we assume that the automaton is deterministic. This can be generalized easily to the nondeterministic case.
* <math>\forall x (\neg\exists y S(x, y)) \to \bigvee_{a \in \text{accepting states}} Q_a(x)   </math>.

=== MSO-expressible implies regular ===
Conversely, to show that each MSO formula defines a language that is regular, it suffices to induct over the syntax of MSO formulas. This boils down to induction over <math>\neg, \wedge </math>, and [[existential quantification]] over monadic predicates. These correspond to complement, intersection, and projection (a restricted kind of homomorphism). The set of regular languages over <math>\Sigma </math> is closed under complement, intersection, and projection.<ref>{{Citation |last=Thomas |first=Wolfgang |chapter=Languages, Automata, and Logic |date=1997 |title=Handbook of Formal Languages |pages=389–455 |editor-last=Rozenberg |editor-first=Grzegorz |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-642-59126-6_7 |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-59126-6_7 |isbn=978-3-642-63859-6 |editor2-last=Salomaa |editor2-first=Arto|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>
